story.title: Judge Dismisses Trump's Defamation Lawsuit Over Epstein Letter
story.summary: A U.S. District Judge has dismissed Donald Trump's $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal regarding a letter he allegedly wrote to Jeffrey Epstein. The judge ruled that Trump failed to demonstrate that the defendants made defamatory statements with actual malice, stating he was 'grasping at straws.' The lawsuit was dismissed with prejudice, meaning Trump cannot refile the case.

event_overview.title: About A federal judge in Florida on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by D
event_overview.subject: A federal judge in Florida on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by D
event_overview.summary: This event is the federal civil case Trump v. British Broadcasting Corporation, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida. President Donald J. Trump alleges that the BBC’s documentary editing of portions of his January 6, 2021 speech was defamatory and violated Florida’s deceptive-and-unfair-trade-practices law; the BBC has denied defaming him.

facts.label: Court and case
facts.value: The case is No. 1:25-cv-25894-ALTMAN/LETT, in the Miami Division of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida; Trump is the plaintiff and the British Broadcasting Corporation is the remaining defendant.

facts.label: Filing and claims
facts.value: Trump filed the action in December 2025, asserting defamation and a claim under Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act in connection with the documentary “Trump: A Second Chance.”

facts.label: Damages and discovery
facts.value: The complaint initially sought at least $5 billion, while Trump later estimated damages at about $10 billion. Because he alleges reputational and business harm, discovery has included requests for financial and Mar-a-Lago membership information.

facts.label: October 2026 procedural posture
facts.value: On October 22, 2026, U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett required Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11 unless the discovery schedule were extended; discovery was then scheduled to end December 18, 2026.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline follows the BBC case’s October 2026 discovery dispute, but its November 1 entry concerns a separate defamation case against The Wall Street Journal over an Epstein-related article, not the BBC litigation.

explore_lenses.label: How did the case reach a final dismissal?
explore_lenses.title: A second pleading fell short
explore_lenses.summary: Trump first sued in July 2025 after the Journal reported on an alleged 2003 birthday-book letter to Jeffrey Epstein. The court initially allowed him to amend, but held that the revised complaint still did not plausibly allege the required state of mind for defamation.

claims.text: Trump sued Dow Jones, News Corp., Rupert Murdoch, Robert Thomson, and Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joseph Palazzolo; the case was filed in the Southern District of Florida in July 2025.
Judge Gayles dismissed the original complaint without prejudice in April 2026 for insufficient allegations of actual malice, giving Trump an opportunity to amend.
The October 31 ruling dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice because Trump had made a second unsuccessful attempt to plead actual malice.

explore_lenses.label: What did the judge decide—and leave open?
explore_lenses.title: The ruling addressed malice, not authorship
explore_lenses.summary: The decision turned on whether Trump plausibly alleged that the defendants knew the reporting was false or recklessly disregarded probable falsity. It did not determine whether Trump wrote the letter or whether every factual assertion in the Journal article was true.

claims.text: Because Trump is a public figure, his defamation claim required plausible allegations of “actual malice”: knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth.
Gayles found the amended allegations of malice conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the article, or irrelevant to whether the defendants knew the reporting was false.
Trump maintained that the letter was fake and that the report was false and defamatory; Dow Jones said it was pleased with the court’s decision.
The court did not decide at the pleading stage whether Trump authored the letter or whether he was Epstein’s friend.

explore_lenses.label: What could happen next?
explore_lenses.title: An appeal and fee fight remain possible
explore_lenses.summary: “With prejudice” prevents Trump from filing the same claim again in the district court, but it does not bar appellate review. His legal team said it plans to appeal, while the order also left open further litigation over defendants’ fees and costs.

claims.text: Trump’s legal team said that he would continue pursuing the case and appeal the dismissal.
The ruling with prejudice bars another refiling of these claims in district court; it does not itself eliminate the normal right to seek review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.
The order retained jurisdiction over potential attorney-fee and cost requests and gave defendants 30 days to file a motion addressing the applicable law, according to reporting based on the order.

story_report.summary: A federal judge in South Florida dismissed with prejudice Donald Trump’s defamation lawsuit over a Wall Street Journal report about a letter to Jeffrey Epstein, after finding that Trump had not plausibly alleged actual malice. The ruling prevents Trump from filing the same claims again in district court, though his legal team said he plans to appeal. The decision did not determine whether Trump wrote the disputed letter or resolve the underlying factual dispute about it.

sections.heading: Trump’s lawsuit against Journal defendants
sections.body: Trump filed the case in the Southern District of Florida in July 2025 against Dow Jones, News Corp., Rupert Murdoch, Robert Thomson and Wall Street Journal reporters Khadeeja Safdar and Joseph Palazzolo. Judge Darrin Gayles had dismissed the original complaint without prejudice in April 2026, finding its allegations of actual malice insufficient and allowing Trump to amend it.

sections.heading: Actual-malice standard drove dismissal
sections.body: As a public figure, Trump needed to plausibly allege that the defendants knew their reporting was false or acted with reckless disregard for its truth. Gayles found the amended complaint’s malice allegations conclusory, vague, at times inconsistent with the article, or irrelevant to what the defendants knew. The Oct. 31 order dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice after a second unsuccessful effort to plead that standard.

sections.heading: Appeal and fee requests remain possible
sections.body: Trump maintained that the letter was fake and the report false and defamatory, while Dow Jones said it was pleased with the decision. A dismissal with prejudice bars refiling these claims in district court but does not remove the ordinary right to seek review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit. The order also retained jurisdiction over potential attorney-fee and cost requests, giving defendants 30 days to file a motion on the applicable law.

unresolved.text: The dismissal for failure to plead actual malice was not a finding that the disputed letter was authentic, that Trump wrote it, or that he was Epstein’s friend.
As of Nov. 1, 2026, the consulted sources did not identify a notice of appeal or a fee motion; the timing and outcome of either remain unknown.

related_stories.title: FBI Links North Korea to $6.3 Billion Binance Crypto Heist
related_stories.summary: The FBI has attributed the recent $6.3 billion hack of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance to North Korea, specifically identifying a group known as TraderTraitor as responsible for the cyber attack. This incident is noted as the largest cryptocurrency theft in history. Following the breach, Binance has resumed withdrawals and reported that it has covered approximately 90% of the losses incurred by its users.
